pr_title: make use of ports in SPN optional
pr_body:
This is regression caused by #40860. There is some ambiguity if port should be used for contracting SPN when it is not default port. We did not do that up to 5.0 and we do since. However that change can have negative impact on existing services. 
Since there is no API for developers to control the SPN (#25320), I added ENV & AppContext switch so control this and choose old or new behavior globally. 

I did some more testing with IIS can 4.7/4.8 It seems like when configure server on custom ports, client connects to it without specifying port in SPN. 
For that reason I'm leaving this off by default as we did prior to 5.0.


fixes #53193
fixes #51701

> It seems that the target service itself should determine how it accepts authentication.

This misunderstands the issue. The sequence is a 401 from the server to client saying it supports Negotiate. There is no facility for the server to tell the client which SPN it should acquire a ticket for, that is left to the client. How that happens varies a bit across platforms (in SSPI applications work directly an SPN, in GSSAPI they usually work a more abstract form) and to some extent applications (the client app has to know the type of service it's trying to access). The result of that in an SPN sent in a TGS-REQ to a KDC, assuming there is no ticket in the cache (and no negative entry). The KDC returns a service ticket, a referral or an error. The client then repeats its HTTP request providing that ticket and providing its knowledge of the session key contained within. In the event that the ticket acquisition fails, Windows will silently fall back to NTLM unless you've disabled it. The point is the only information the server ever gets to tell the client is "I support Negotiate authentication", all other communication is between the client and KDC. 

> Triage: This seems to be according to the spec. The fact 3.1 was working was a bug. We will document it as breaking change.

Which spec says this? There is no mention of port numbers in https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4559 and what is  implemented in .NET 5.0 is contrary to the behavior of .NET Framework, previous versions of .NET Core, every major browser and curl. At least contrary to the default behavior without custom policies applied. Chrome and IE have support for including the port if a non-standard policy is applied.
any thoughts on this @SteveSyfuhs?

There's no good answer here. In an ideal world the client already knows the SPN and doesn't glean it from the URL.

> The point is the only information the server ever gets to tell the client is "I support Negotiate authentication", all other communication is between the client and KDC.

This is actually the critical bit of information here. This is done for security reasons, otherwise an attacker-controlled service can just specify an SPN other than the service you connected to, and do all manner of evil things (this protection _must_ assume no TLS).

I'm not aware of any IETF spec that explicitly states a port is required in the SPN or not. It's happily underspecified, leading to this mess. The port _should_ be on the SPN if it's a non-standard service port. That's important for all sorts of high-density scenarios. However, because SPNs aren't easily modified in AD (i.e. requiring admins), the application should have the option to toggle this behavior off. As I recall we collectively landed on not including the port _by default_.

I agree that this is under-specified. The whole thing is a retcon of IE behavior that was only later turned into an RFC. In the absence of a spec stating that the port should be included, the precedent set by existing implementations should be the default behavior.

A facility to alter that default makes some amount of sense if you want to offer it. Any environment using ports in SPNs for HTTP services has already opted themselves into turning knobs in their browsers, curl and other things. Having to opt in to get that behavior in .NET seems reasonable.

Re:density - there are a number of ways to solve that. Additional A records are one of the more traditional ones.

I also look at the code again and if `Host:` header is set we would use it as is and we would bypass the logic that tries to calculate SPN using port.

The automatic downgrade to NTLM is a Windows/SSPI behavior rather than something being done explicitly by .NET. The only thing .NET really gets to choose here is the SPN it passes to SSPI. From that point on it’s basically just shuffling blobs between buffers returned from SSPI APIs and HTTP headers. .NET could examine the attributes of an established context, and that would imply whether the SPN it used was “correct” I guess, but it’s not clear what it would do with that information.

I would advise against applying any logic that checks on which protocol gets negotiated, except maybe to optionally fail unsafe protocols like NTLM. Any allow-only list is going to hurt in the long run when we add another nego protocol. That said, any such prevention should happen before the negotiation happens. There's existing Windows policies that disable NTLM as mentioned previously.

> I would advise against applying any logic that checks on which protocol gets negotiated

Agreed - whether NTLM is "OK" for someone's environment is better controlled at the OS level rather than within an application. The GP options for auditing/disabling NTLM are fairly good/granular. Using negotiate at all implies some amount of cooperation between app developers and security/infra teams that typically manage those.

> I also look at the code again and if Host: header is set we would use it as is and we would bypass the logic that tries to calculate SPN using port.

That is useful to know, but not always a viable workaround to restore the Core 3.1/Framework behavior. In many scenarios there are layers of libraries and abstractions that make it cumbersome/impractical to set custom values for headers. Even where it is possible to do so, it requires more invasive changes than one might hope for when rebuilding a codebase against a newer version of .NET.

My contention is that:
* In the absence of any spec that says otherwise, the 3.1/Framework behavior should be restored. There does not appear to be a clear justification for the breaking change and reverting would bring .NET back in line with curl and browsers regarding this behavior.
* If an opt-in for ports in SPNs is desired, it should be a new property on `HttpClientHandler` or an opt in global switch for the app or something along those lines.

>

Just setting "Host: " header with the right host is all it took to send Negotiate.  I didn't have to have the port.  I tried setting it to a couple of other things, but the only thing that made it send Negotiate is it I set to the host of the URL I was calling.

> host.domain.com is an Alias. I think It's a CNAME record

Kerberos clients typically canonicalize hostnames before forming the SPN. Canonicalize meaning that CNAMEs are resolved and the name in the A they point to is used, and that any DNS suffix that was appended to resolve the name is included. Because SSPI expects the client to provide the SPN as a literal string, this canonicalization is an application behavior/convention on Windows. In GSSAPI, where forming the actual SPN is done by the GSSAPI implementation, this is generally controlled by system-level configuration (e.g. in MIT `dns_canonicalize_hostname` in `krb5.conf`, which defaults to true (see [here](https://web.mit.edu/kerberos/krb5-1.12/doc/admin/conf_files/krb5_conf.html)).

Since in SSPI, applications are more free to deviate, they sometimes do. The SMB client in more recent versions of Windows for instance explicitly does *not* canonicalize hostnames before forming an SPN. All major Kerberized HTTP implementations that I am aware of do canonicalize hostnames in SPNs. Chrome accidentally stopped doing this a few years back and quickly fixed the bug to restore the canonicalizing behavior, see the [bug here](https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=872665). Once in a while, you'll see something that was primarily developed for Unix systems, where canonicalization was done automatically by their GSSAPI library, ported to Windows, where it's now the responsibility of the application/HTTP library. In those cases, not canonicalizing seems to be an oversight rather than intentional behavior.

Anyway, regarding canonicalization, .NET appears to be in line with other implementations. The inclusion of the port is something else, but the host name portion is correct. The SPN of the server principal should be `HTTP/fqdn`, where `fqdn` is the canonicalized FQDN of the server, not a CNAME.

> Is there a guide on enabling tracing

If you want to know "what" it's doing, a packet capture (ports 53 and 88, UDP and TCP, plus your HTTP traffic if you want that) is generally the easiest way to see, at least on Windows. Just be sure to `klist purge` and `ipconfig /flushdns` first. If you fail to do this, various positive and negative caches will be in play and you may not actually see the relevant Kerberos and DNS traffic on the wire. If you want to know "why", then you'd need tracing on the .NET side, which I'll leave to others. On Unix (at least with MIT), setting the env var `KRB5_TRACE=/dev/stderr` and then running your reproducer is a quick and easy way to trace Kerberos activity.

Since this is somewhat ambiguous my plan is to add context switch so application can choose the behavior. That it self should not be too difficult. The major obstacle at this point is building test environment and verification.

I wanted to add an additional finding that I discovered. This broke a WCF test scenario so I used the work around of specifying the Host header to override what SPN is used. I tried to capture the request through fiddler, but proxy servers use the Host header to forward the request. So if using a proxy server, the mechanism provided to override the SPN won't work as it causes the proxy server to connect on the default port. So basically .NET 5 can't be used with a server on a non-default port with Kerberos authentication through a proxy server. I know proxies to HTTPS servers use SSL tunneling, but Kerberos is also valid for HTTP. With the .NET 3.1 behavior, if the port number was needed in the SPN, adding it via the Host header wouldn't break anything. There's also the possibility a server implementation might pay too much attention to the Host header and misdirect the request, especially with a reverse proxy frontend.

Is there any news on doing something for issue #25320? WCF recently implemented WSFederation and we're going to be adding a WSTrustChannelFactory very soon. What this means is we're going to be used more for making requests to ADFS servers requiring Kerberos authentication, and [by default](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-server-2012-R2-and-2012/dn554247(v=ws.11)) HOST and not HTTP is used for the service name part of the SPN that an ADFS server is using. I know HTTP is usually an alias for HOST, but it doesn't have to be. The Host header based fudge that exists is insufficient for these scenarios. And we still can't use UPN's.

I did more testing with IIS & 4.8. (targeting 4.7)
I set up IIS on non-default port and tried to connect with .NET Framework. 
And it works without sending port in SPN. 

Since there is still some ambiguity I added code to decide with AppContext & ENV and I set it off by default e.g. no port to match my observed behavior. (we probably should have done more investigation for #36644) 
Who ever needs it can set either `System.Net.Http.UsePortInSpn` or `DOTNET_SYSTEM_NET_HTTP_USEPORTINSPN` and get the 5.0 behavior. 

To me the big question is what should be do for 5.0. 
Since 6.0 is near by and becoming LTS we can choose to do nothing.
